I was born and raised in the bustling quarter of Tsinga, right on the edge of the CENAT neighborhood in Yaoundé. Growing up there, I learned to navigate the narrow streets and the rhythm of the market stalls that line the main road. My family has lived here for generations, and the smell of fresh plantain and the hum of radio music have always been part of my daily life.

I’m a 30‑year‑old woman who works as a part‑time sales assistant at the local market in CENAT. My job is modest; I earn just under 30,000 CFA francs a month, enough to cover my rent, a few groceries, and the occasional outing with my sister. Even with a tight budget, I try to keep a sense of community by helping my neighbors with small chores and sharing stories over steaming cups of palm wine.

Last week, I took a short trip to Nkollesseng, specifically the Petit !Tre Paris area, to visit my mother who lives there. The journey was simple: I hopped on the city bus at 8 a.m., the same bus that carries students and workers from all over Yaoundé. The ride was a mix of city traffic and the occasional stop for a street vendor. Arriving at Nkollesseng, I was greeted by the familiar scent of roasted beans and the sight of my mother’s garden, a patchwork of vegetables and herbs that she tends with such care.

The purpose of my trip was simple: to return home. I spent the day catching up with my family, helping my mother with household chores, and sharing a meal of grilled fish and fufu. In the evening, as the sun set over the hills of Nkollesseng, I reflected on the closeness of our family ties and the importance of staying connected, even when my work keeps me busy in CENAT.

I return to Yaoundé every week, balancing my responsibilities at the market with my love for my family and the vibrant life of my neighborhood. Life here may not be glamorous, but it is rich with community, resilience, and the simple joys of everyday living.

I was born and raised in the bustling quarter of Quatier Aoussà in the Onana district of Yaoundé. Growing up, the narrow streets and the constant hum of motorbikes shaped my early memories. My family lives in a modest apartment on Rue des Palmiers, and we share a small kitchen where my mother still cooks her famous ndolé. I attended the local primary school, then moved on to the lycée in the neighboring district, where I excelled in mathematics and French.

After finishing secondary school at the age of 18, I decided to stay in Yaoundé to pursue a career in logistics. I secured a part-time position at a local courier company, handling package deliveries across the city. The job pays less than 30,000 CFA per month, but it allows me to support my parents and save a little for my future. Every morning, I walk from my apartment to the company office, passing the bustling market stalls and the old colonial buildings that give Onana its unique charm.

My daily routine is simple yet fulfilling: I start my shift at 7 a.m., loading parcels onto the company van, and by late afternoon, I’m back home, helping my younger brother with his schoolwork. Despite the modest income, I enjoy the sense of independence and the opportunity to build a career in a city that never stops moving. I am proud of my roots in Quatier Aoussà and hopeful that one day I’ll be able to invest back into the community that has shaped me.

Je m’appelle Jean‑Baptiste Nguema, j’ai 48 ans et je vis à Mokolo, l’un des quartiers les plus animés de Yaoundé. Je suis né et j’ai grandi à proximité de l’École Publique de Me Saa, un établissement qui a toujours été le cœur de notre voisinage. J’ai passé mon enfance à jouer dans les ruelles étroites de Mokolo, à écouter les histoires de mes grands‑parents et à admirer le coucher de soleil sur la petite place où se réunissent les commerçants du quartier.

Je suis marié à Awa, une femme forte et débrouillarde, et nous avons deux enfants, un garçon de 12 ans et une fille de 9 ans. Je travaille comme vendeur ambulant dans le marché de la ville, un métier qui me permet de gagner un revenu mensuel d’environ 28 000 FCFA. Ce salaire est suffisant pour subvenir aux besoins de ma famille, mais il ne me laisse pas beaucoup de marge pour les économies. Malgré ces contraintes, j’ai appris à gérer mon budget avec rigueur, en privilégiant les achats essentiels et en cherchant toujours les meilleures affaires.

Chaque semaine, je me rends au Petit Marché Carrefour Lumière, situé dans le quartier de Carrefour Lumière, pour faire les courses de la famille. Ce marché est proche de mon lieu de travail et offre une grande variété de produits à des prix raisonnables. J’y trouve tout ce dont j’ai besoin : légumes frais, épices, poissons et parfois des articles ménagers. J’apprécie l’ambiance conviviale du marché et l’opportunité de rencontrer les vendeurs que je connais depuis longtemps. Faire mes courses à Carrefour Lumière est un rituel que je ne manque jamais, car c’est à la fois pratique et économique.
